utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four very short matters of report. First; the witness Vasiljkovic, called last week, made serious allegations about the OTP as the Chamber will recall. He's been repeating them and enlarging them in the press. Quite inappropriate, of course, for the OTP to make any comments on such matters, however, the Court should know that after he left last week and when it was possible to locate him, he was informed not only, of course, that he would no longer be contacted in relation to his evidence but that there would be an inquiry into the allegations that he was making at which he would be invited to take part. That remains the position. The Chamber will be informed of the result of inquiries one way or another in -- of that inquiry one way or the other in due course and we will seek to call the evidence that I spoke of last week. Second, I think we are awaiting a decision in respect of the 92 bis'ing of C-032 in part and respectfully ask that we can hear about that because he's coming up soon. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: C-032. Is that in the large group that we had?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'll need some assistance on that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The legal officer kindly reminds us it's in the last application. We may be able to have a look at that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'd be very grateful. I'm going to be in and out today but on procedural matters I or, in this case, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will come and deal with it, if necessary. The Vukovar motion will be in today because we know you want to deal with that. And the fourth and last point is that there is a report on contempt, a further report on contempt by a Montenegrin newspaper that you wanted for us. We've been unable to take the matter any further, and we'll give, as it were, a nil return report in relation to that today or very soon. Mr. Groome will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I seem to be having some trouble with my headphones. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Ambassador Herbert Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, there are three volumes of exhibits which I will be working with with the ambassador. It will please the Court, I'd ask we assign them exhibit numbers now. The first binder is a group of UN documents as well as some other miscellaneous documents. It's the soft cover blue binder that you have. The second one is the seven notebooks which together comprise diaries for the Vance mission to Yugoslavia from October 1991 until May of 1992. And binder three are nine notebooks which together comprise Ambassador Okun's diaries for the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia from September of 1992 until May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, allow the witness to take the declaration and we'll then deal with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take the declaration, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could deal with these exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Volume 1 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 396, Volume 2 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 397, and Volume 3 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the witness has a limited amount of time in which he can be available; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, by Friday afternoon. He has a class to teach on Monday. He has informed me that, if necessary, he will cancel that class but would prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And we also have another witness to interpose tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So effectively, we've got two days and perhaps a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if you'd bear that in mind, of course, when taking the witness in chief. If you can deal with that as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In order to expedite the taking of the evidence in chief, there are a number of meetings referred to in the summary which I will not adduce evidence, live testimony. I believe the diary entries are self-explanatory and clear, and I would believe -- I would draw the Chamber's attention to these specific diary entries but I will not be asking the ambassador specific questions regarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Ambassador, if you want to take a break at any time, tell us and we can adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before I start, Your Honour, I would also inform the Court that we will be using this Sanction system again. So although the Chamber does have hard copies of all the diary entries, the particular page that I will be referring to with the ambassador will also appear on the computer screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's called the Sanction system?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sanction II is the name of the computer programme that puts it up on the screen. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, I would like to begin by asking you about your background and career as a diplomat. In order to expedite this, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 1, and it will be displayed on the screen in front you. If you can read it clearly, I'd ask you, do you recognise what is depicted on the screen in front of you? The screen should be placed to "off" for the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It is my biographic entry in Who's Who in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read it and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, with one minor change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was the entry for the year 2001, and it shows me as a -- correctly as a member of the -- US member of the UN International Narcotics Control Board. My term ended in 2002, so I am no longer a member of the board. Otherwise, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you to briefly describe -- or perhaps I'll read to you a paragraph regarding some of the more salient parts of your career and ask you to agree or disagree with what I read afterwards. Is it true that you had a long career in international diplomacy, that you served as an officer in the United States Foreign Service from 1955 until 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the early 1960s, while serving in the US embassy in Moscow during the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, you were the person responsible for translating the letters from Chairman Kruschev to President Kennedy. In the late 1970s, you were deputy chairman of the US delegation at the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks with the Soviet Union, commonly known as SALT II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first appointed as an ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In 1980, to the German Democratic Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that post?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I served in Berlin from 1980 to 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation to catch up. From 1985 to 1989, what post did you hold?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I was deputy permanent representative and ambassador of the United States to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1997, did you serve in the capacity as the special advisor and the deputy to the personal envoy of the UN Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what issues did you work in relation to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1993, primarily Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. From 1993 to 1997, we worked primarily, almost exclusively, on the dispute between Greece and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From September of 1992 until May of 1993, were you the deputy co-chairman of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1996 to 1997, were you special advisor to the International Commission on Missing Persons in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, in addition to what is in tab 1 of Prosecution Exhibit 396 and what we've discussed here, have you had any teaching positions?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: During most of the 1990s, I was a visiting lecturer on international law at the Yale Law School in Connecticut in the US, and at present I'm a professorial lecturer on international relations, international law, and international institutions at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University in Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, I would ask you at this stage, could you please give the Chamber with a little greater detail the role and responsibilities you played in Yugoslavia during the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Secretary Vance and I were the representatives of the Secretary-General. The initial responsibility began in October of 1991 when there was heavy fighting in Croatia, and we went there initially to see the situation, to find out the facts, and then to determine and recommend to the Secretary-General and to the Security Council of the UN a course of action. In Bosnia, the situation was more complex, more difficult, and the situation there was the matter of a conference, but recommending a course Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of action and deciding what to do was the same principle. And between Greece and Macedonia, the issue was to avert a conflict between them and, if we could, as we did, reach a peaceful settlement of the dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 1990s, had you ever had occasion to be in Yugoslavia or have a job in connection with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe for us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I first visited Yugoslavia in 1957 as a tourist. I travelled throughout the country. In the middle 1970s, specifically 1973, 1974, I was political advisor to the NATO Commander-in-Chief in the Mediterranean, based in Naples, with the specific responsibility of watching and reporting on the situation in Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you met him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The first time was December 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe just briefly the circumstances surrounding your meeting with Mr. Milosevic at that time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I was travelling with a group of senior American officials and businessmen, including Secretary -- former Secretary of State Vance under the auspices of the Financial Services Volunteer Corps. This is an organisation we had founded, a not-for-profit organisation that worked on bringing free market institutions to former communist countries, and we were there to examine and discuss the political situation in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to meeting Mr. Milosevic, did you meet other federal and republican government officials?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we met them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your first set of missions to the area as the deputy to the special envoy of the UN Secretary-General, can you describe, just in a summary fashion, when those missions took place.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, they began in early October of 1991 and extended through June of 1992. The heaviest period of involvement was between October and January when Secretary Vance achieved a cessation of hostilities in Croatia and the entry of a peacekeeping force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we talk about specific meetings in relation to that mission, can you assist us by telling us, what was the culminating act or work product of that series of missions?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The culmination was the implementing accord of January 2, 1992, which implemented a previous tentative cease-fire agreement and that effectively ended the war, brought about a cessation of hostilities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this series of missions, did you then embark on a second series of missions to the region?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the times and the mandate of that series of missions.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We went back again - that is Secretary Vance and I - at the very beginning of October, the first days of October 1992, when fighting began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then there was a hiatus, but beginning with the London conference in August of 1992 which led to the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia a week later, in September, we were involved continuously in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina and still somewhat marginally on the issues involving the peacekeeping operation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the culminating act or work product of this series of missions?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The conference's culminating act, as you describe it, was the development and presentation to the parties of the political settlement for the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the so-called Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that peace plan, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, ultimately adopted by all of the parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which party did not, or rejected it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was accepted by the Bosnian Croats and by the Bosnian Muslims, and it was ultimately rejected by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of these two sets of missions, did you keep records regarding the meetings that you had with the principals involved?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what method of record-keeping you employed.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I took notes of all the meetings we attended at the time the meetings occurred. The diaries, the notebooks are here at my side. And I did that regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that for every mission, there is an individual notebook that you created to record what you heard?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's correct. That is how I organised the work product.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was every meeting recorded in your diaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Every meeting that I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the notes -- are you the sole author of the material in your diaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were your notes made contemporaneously with, when the meetings were going on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the diaries reflect the statements of many of the principal political and military leaders involved in the break-up of Yugoslavia, inter alia, the federal Yugoslav authorities, the presidents of the republics, local Serb leaders in Croatia, Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Serb, and Bosnian Croat leaders as well as Albanian leaders in Kosovo and Albania, Macedonians and Montenegrins? Do your diaries include records of meetings with all of those people?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the diaries also record the times when Secretary Vance and yourself notified these leaders of crimes that were being committed by people on their side or under their control?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these meetings that you had, did some of the other parties also have note-takers?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Intermittently some of the other parties did. Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your diary notes form the basis of Secretary Vance's reports to the Secretary-General of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the diaries after you completed your mission?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I kept them in my possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have they ever been published or been made the subject of any published work?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you willing to make them available to the Chamber to use as evidence in this case or any other case before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, to assist the Chamber in reading the diaries, did you work with a member of the Prosecution staff to create a glossary of the -- of terms that you used in the diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the ambassador be shown Prosecution Exhibit 34 -- 396, tab 2, and I would note for the Chamber that footnote 3 in the witness summary contains some last-minute corrections to typographical errors that Ambassador Okun made late yesterday, after the exhibit was processed. So I'd ask the Chamber to read both the glossary in conjunction with footnote 3 in the witness summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the glossary that you worked to create to assist the Chamber in deciphering the diaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could help me to find the witness summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. There were some typographical errors in the exhibit that the witness has. Those corrections are in footnote 3, and it is on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness summary is marked -- we're asking it be marked for identification as tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And footnote 3, if you would tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's on page 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, did you also work with a member of the Prosecution staff to create a schedule of an index to some of the more important or significant meetings in the diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 4 -- no, I'm sorry; tab 3. Is that a -- the index of important meetings that you helped create to assist the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would like to now ask you about some specific meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would note, for the Chamber, that I will be skipping the first meeting in the summary and proceeding directly to paragraph 13 of the witness summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to draw your attention to a meeting of the 13th of October, 1991. Did you meet with Mr. Milosevic in his office on that day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your meetings with Mr. Milosevic, what language was used?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He normally spoke English. He speaks very good English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic -- was there ever a translator used that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would Mr. Milosevic have been able to see you taking the notes that you took during your meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you to summarise what occurred during this first meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At that first meeting, which was between a meeting with the Federal Prime Minister, the then Federal Prime Minister Ante Markovic, and General Kadijevic, at that meeting, President Milosevic, of course, greeted Secretary Vance courteously and discussed the situation in the country. Secretary Vance had some questions, and President Milosevic answered them. Specifically, he told us that he disclaimed responsibility or control, one might say, over the JNA or over the Rump Presidency, and he spoke at some length about the crimes he described that were being committed against the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Secretary Vance and yourself attempted to verify some of the information that Mr. Milosevic presented to you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to verify it as true or false?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the -- on the matter of control of the JNA and the Rump Presidency, the fact was that President Milosevic was the controlling factor. He did control the JNA de facto, and also he controlled the Rump Presidency of Yugoslavia, which was then basically Serbia and Montenegro, and he certainly was the man in charge. We never were able to verify the descriptions of the thousands of Serbs being killed. Of course, there were Serbs being killed in Croatia, but the overwhelming number of fatalities were Croatians being killed by the Serbs. So the situation was really the reverse to that he described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After meeting with Mr. Milosevic, did you meet with General Veljko Kadijevic and General Adzic on the same day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not go -- ask the ambassador specific questions about this, but I would draw the Chamber's attention to the diary entries relevant to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think in order that we can have it on the record and to help us find our way through, if on each of these occasions you refer to the diary entry so that we have a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I see, for instance, that the first meeting you referred to, the diary appears to be 397, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it was page 47, as marked in the diary, not the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 47 of the diary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first set of diaries were numbered by Ambassador Okun, so you would be correct. It's 397, tab 1, page 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first meeting that I skipped, Your Honour, with respect to Prime Minister Ante Markovic, that would be Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 1, page 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, could you assist us: With respect to the meeting you had with Veljko Kadijevic, General Kadijevic, what page in the diary was that meeting noted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I see it begins on diary page 54 and ends on page 63. Pages 54 to 63 of the diary in the Vance mission book number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 4. Do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if that could be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is depicted in that picture?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It's a picture of President Milosevic and me, talking together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was this picture taken, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was taken in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it taken during one of the meetings that you had with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Probably in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, I'd like to now draw your attention to the Carrington Draft Convention on the 18th of October, 1991, an event that you recorded in your diaries, which would be 397, tab 1, page 131. Can you please describe for the Chamber what the Carrington Draft Convention was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The so-called Carrington Draft Convention was the culminating document of the EC-sponsored - that's the European Community's - Conference on Yugoslavia. Throughout conflict in Croatia and the first six months of the conflict in Bosnia, that is from the summer of 1991 until September of 1992, the diplomatic negotiations for a settlement were led by the European Community. The conference that they called, which all Yugoslav parties participated in, was called the Conference on Yugoslavia, although it was given other names by the press. And Lord Carrington, the former British Foreign Secretary, was the chairman of the conference. In October, on the 18th of October, Lord Carrington, after consultation with all the Yugoslav parties, presented a plan for an overall comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav conflict, and that was called the Agreed General Settlement, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to show you Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 5. I'd ask you to take a look at it and ask you whether you recognise what this document is.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document of 18 October 1991 of Lord Carrington. Excuse me, I was incorrect in its name. It's not the Agreement for General Settlement, it's called Arrangements for General Settlement. Arrangements for General Settlement. It was, in effect, a framework agreement for a peace treaty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the respective parties adopt this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was accepted by all of the Yugoslav republics except one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which republic rejected it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the Serb delegation do on the 18th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They -- the Serb delegation at the conference walked out. That is, they physically got up out of their seats and left the conference room; a walkout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself form an opinion regarding the significance of what happened on the 18th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what that was.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I felt and believed at the time that the Serb walkout was a very serious blow to the conference and signalled the fact that Serbia alone among the Yugoslav republics was the one that wished the war to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where was this conference, Ambassador? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was it held?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have a number of conferences and we're trying to get them into order. We have a number of plans which we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may take a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of the conference was the Conference on Yugoslavia, but it was often referred to by the city in which it was held. This particular meeting in October 1991 was held in The Hague and was often referred to in the press and by others as The Hague Peace Conference. The reason it was held in The Hague was that the Dutch government at that time held the rotating presidency of the EC. When the presidency moved on January 1, 1992, to Portugal, the conference then shifted to Brussels. So it became the Brussels Peace Conference, to the press and to the public at large. But it was always and we always referred to it, for ease of reference and accuracy, as the Conference on Yugoslavia, namely, the EC-sponsored conference under Lord Carrington's chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We in fact have had evidence about this, but I don't think as clearly as we're getting it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, are there other conferences that have popular designations because of where they were held that officially were part of this EC initiative named the Conference on Yugoslavia? You've told us about the Hague Peace Conference and the Brussels Peace Conference. Were there any others that fall within the ambit of the Conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please can you tell us those.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: There were several others. When the conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina in March of 1992, Lord Carrington appointed a Portuguese diplomat, a very able Portuguese diplomat, Ambassador Jose Cutilheiro, to head a smaller conference specifically on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You will recall that the Conference on Yugoslavia was an overall conference. It concerned all of Yugoslavia. So Lord Carrington asked Ambassador Cutilheiro to work specifically on the conflict in Bosnia. That subconference was often referred to as the Cutilheiro Conference or the Lisbon Conference, depending on where they met, but it was an adjunct to the Carrington Conference on Yugoslavia. It was the Bosnian addendum, if you will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other conferences that fall within the ambit of the Conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the final conference was called by the British government in August 1992 when the UK had taken the presidency of the European Community, and that was the final conference of the EC-sponsored effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, while we're talking on this subject, would it be fair to say that at some point when the Conference on Yugoslavia ended, there was a broader initiative of conferences that involved not just the EC but other nations as well as EC members?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, there were, to the degree that the UN became increasingly involved throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name that's attributed to that set of conferences that began after the Conference on Yugoslavia completed its work?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, immediately after the London conference of August 1992 -- at the London conference, the decision was made to end the EC effort, the solo effort of the European Community. Out of the London conference came a combined EC-United Nations effort. That was the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia which began its work in September 1992 and continued until about 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, unlike the Conference on Yugoslavia, did the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, did that have more or less a base of operations or a location from which it conducted most of its business?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The conference had a headquarters from which it did all its business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this particular conference commonly referred to by its initials I-C-F-Y or ICFY?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Incidentally, the headquarters was Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw you back now to the 6th of November, 1991. Did you have a meeting with the Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to open up your diary to that page. And which mission is this, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: This was during the second -- our second mission to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 2, page 32. Can I ask you to first briefly summarise what occurred during this meeting with Prime Minister Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He made some important statements and comments on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation. At least, we found them important. He told us that the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, the federal army, was becoming increasingly Serbianised, as he put it, as an army of Serbia. He also mentioned that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were acting in a secessionist way and that Presidents Tudjman and Milosevic were planning to divide Bosnia between them, that is between Serbia and Croatia. He mentioned that the European Community still believed the problem could be resolved quickly but that he thought they were quite wrong on that matter, that the problem was more difficult than the EC thought. And I believe he spoke about the JNA arming Serb irregulars and paramilitaries in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to draw your attention to the top half of page 32, and I'm going to ask you just to describe some of the nomenclature that you used when you recorded people's statements so that the Chamber can accurately interpret what it was you were recording. There you have "CRV," and it has a line saying, "I worry about Serbia and Croatia." "CRV" stands for who?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: "CRV" is Secretary Vance. His name is Cyrus Roberts Vance, and I would use the initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And incidentally, is it true that Secretary Vance has since died?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, underneath that, there is the word "Mark," underlined, and then a passage. "Mark" refers to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: "Mark" is Prime Minister Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the passage, beginning with, "They already discussed it, i.e., dividing of B-H..." some of it appears in quotes. The word "secessionist" appears in quotes. The remainder does not. Can you please describe for the Chamber what is the significance, how should they interpret the text that's not in quotes and how should they interpret the text that is in quotes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, throughout the diaries, I was writing them as the individuals were speaking. Throughout the diaries, the text not in quotes is an almost exact quote. It's a very, very close paraphrase of what was said, usually the exact words. When something seemed particularly important and I heard the words, the words were used, I would put it inside quotes, so that everything inside quotes was said, and I heard it and noted it in quotes. So if the word "secessionist" is quoted, it means he used the word "secessionist." But rest of the sentence would be also accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of your early meetings with members or presidents of the respective republics and other military leaders that you met, did Secretary Vance and yourself form an opinion as regarding what you might achieve that would assist the peace process or the peace negotiations that were being conducted under Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe what it was you believed could assist.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We came to the conclusion fairly early on that the creation and imposition of a peacekeeping force, that is to say the creation of a peacekeeping operation and the subsequent imposition of a peacekeeping force in Croatia could materially assist Lord Carrington in his efforts to reach a political settlement of the conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during one of the missions that -- or -- I'll withdraw that. Was the purpose of one of the missions to Yugoslavia to go and present these ideas to the respective parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That happened in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the first person that you presented these ideas to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The first person was President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I draw your attention to a meeting of the 18th of November, 1991, and that would be in your book 3, or Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 3, page 40 is where the meeting begins. Is that the meeting at which these ideas were first presented to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, as I ask you to describe what transpired during that meeting, you'll note that pages 42 and 43 are presented on the monitor for the parties and the Chamber to view. Can you please describe for us what occurred during the course of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was an important and lengthy meeting. We met with President Milosevic and Mr. Jovanovic for about two hours, and Secretary Vance, and we outlined the parameters of a possible peacekeeping operation to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The plan that was presented to Mr. Milosevic, did it differ materially from other UN peacekeeping plans?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what way did it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It differed significantly from all other previous UN peacekeeping operations since it did not involve a mere separation of the parties, a so-called green line across the frontline of a battlefield, but rather it involved what we labelled an inkblot technique. That is the creation of UN peacekeeping force areas that were not contiguous in Croatia and which had the purpose of protecting the Serb population and the Croatian population from the ravages of war, and these became the, and were called, United Nations Protected Areas in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those areas commonly referred to by their initials, U-N-P-A, or UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of this meeting, was the plan fully explained to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The outline of the plan was fully explained to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his reaction, if any, to the plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: His immediate reaction was to say that the plan was fully acceptable to him and to Yugoslavia. Those words are noted at the bottom of page 40 of the diary, and the quote is: "Completely suitable for what we have in Yugoslavia." That was President Milosevic's immediate reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Milosevic asked what General Veljko Kadijevic's reaction would be to such a proposal?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vance asked him that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The president responded that General Kadijevic would agree to the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, at this point in time, had the plan been presented to General Kadijevic or to anybody who in turn might have presented it to General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, it had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please continue with what occurred during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, President Milosevic, as I indicated, said that General Kadijevic would agree. There was some discussion of whether the full former Yugoslav Presidency of eight members or the Rump Presidency of four members would be the overall authorising force, but that was not really an issue. President Milosevic continued on by saying that, "We in Serbia did not allow any irregular or paramilitary troops," but he did acknowledge that in the Eastern Krajinas there were, as he put it, "some local Serbs" who were working with the JNA and helping them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just to take you back, you have, "We in Serbia did not allow any irregular or paramilitary troops," in quotes. So does that indicate that those were the very words Mr. Milosevic used?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in the meeting was Mr. Milosevic asked about the command structure that existed in the Krajinas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He was asked about the command structure in the Croatian Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what he told you and Secretary Vance.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that Babic and Goran Hadzic were both the political and military leaders in the Croatian Krajinas. They were the local Serb political and military leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else with respect to those two men?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He discussed their attitude towards the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said they would represent no problem. He was quite confident on that point, and said, "You can believe me, they will not represent a problem vis-a-vis a proposed peacekeeping operation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred next during the course of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He also mentioned at the meeting that 20 Serb villages in Croatia had recently been razed and burned to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Secretary Vance request any additional information regarding these villages?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We asked him whether a list of the villages or maps could be provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he ever provide those maps or a list of village names?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said he would provide the maps, but we never received them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vance -- the plan that you were presenting on this day, did it call for the prompt demilitarisation of these U-N-P-As or UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was an essential feature of the plan, was to demilitarise the UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this demilitarisation discussed with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that the demilitarisation might take longer than we had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you interpret that statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, I interpreted it at the time - and I note here that I put a red star next to it in the diary and underlined it - as indicating possible non-compliance with the terms of the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would draw your attention to page 48. Towards the end of this meeting, did Mr. Milosevic make a final assertion regarding the position of the Serbian side and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. At the conclusion of the meeting, President Milosevic said, reiterated, that the Serbian side and the JNA would accept and agree to a UN peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he used the term "Serbian side," what did you take that to mean? What parties did that include in your mind?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, in our judgement, it would have included the JNA, as he mentioned explicitly, and the "Serbian side" would have included the Serb irregulars and paramilitaries; Arkan's men, Seselj's men, the White Eagles, those fellows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, would it be fair to say that the successful implementation of what you were proposing would have required the agreement of a -- quite a number of different parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, yes and no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It would have required a number of parties to the degree that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were isolated irregular units fighting the irregulars and the paramilitaries, as they were referred to by all people. Clearly one would need the approval of the Yugoslav government, Serbian government, the Croatian government, the JNA, the Croatian armed forces. But essentially, it boiled down to the approval of Croatia - that is President Tudjman - and Serbia - that is President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time this meeting had concluded, did Secretary Vance and yourself believe that Mr. Milosevic had assured you of the agreement of a number of parties other than himself individually?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explicitly tell us which parties you believed Mr. Milosevic had committed to this plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We believed at the time, and I still believe correctly, that the president had committed himself, the Yugoslav government, the JNA, and the paramilitaries and the irregulars, as well as the local Serb leadership, Goran Hadzic and Milan Babic, to the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that this was a long meeting. Was there any time during the meeting during which there was a break during which Mr. Milosevic would have been able to, perhaps outside of your presence, use a telephone and contact some of these different people or parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. I don't think he ever broke up a meeting to telephone somebody or seek advice or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he at any time express to you the necessity of having to discuss this matter with some of these parties and the need to perhaps get back to you regarding a future course of action?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he qualify the assurances he gave you with any statement to the effect that it would depend on further negotiations or discussions with these parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. I would say to the contrary; he was quite confident in what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, after this meeting, who was the next -- what was the very next meeting that you had?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The next meeting was with the Defence Minister, General Kadijevic. He was accompanied by Admiral Brovet and Colonel Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could draw the Chamber's attention to Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 3, page 50. Ambassador, could you please describe what occurred during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, we outlined again, for General Kadijevic, the proposed peacekeeping operation, and he responded. He responded very quickly and briefly. He really didn't question any aspect of it. His principal question was how long it would take before the decision to deploy the peacekeepers was made. By that, he meant how long from the acceptance and the composition of the force would it take, and one would have to add the approval of the Security Council, how long it would take for the troops physically to arrive in Croatia. That was his concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of this meeting, did the general express any reservations or any limitation upon the people under his control?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. He said the JNA would -- would comply, and he had already told us that the JNA command structure was complete and functioning, that there were no rogue elements within the JNA. He had made that point to us earlier and repeatedly, so he said it again in discussing the possible peacekeeping operation. And he did make one other point which I considered quite important. He said that the army would be fully cooperative, and I quoted him here on page 54 of diary number 3, that the army would be fully cooperative "within its competence." And I noted in brackets, which was a note to myself and for Secretary Vance, I wrote, "nota bene, possible loophole, watch."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the possible loophole that you believe this statement might be referring to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, clearly, to me, it signalled that he was in advance going to disclaim responsibility for any continued action by the Serb paramilitaries and irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of this mission, did Secretary Vance and yourself make the decision to go visit Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe for us the history or the motivation behind your intending to go see Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Vukovar, a city of 50.000 or 60.000 people on the Danube, an important city, had been under siege by the JNA since August. There were many reports -- we received them, of course, from the press but also from the principal humanitarian organisations that were active in Croatia. At the time, there were only two that were seriously active, the International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC, and UNHCR, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and we were receiving reports from them of heavy destruction and of a very serious situation in Vukovar, and we decided that we had to see for ourselves what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We went in vehicles of the JNA. They took us in armoured personnel carriers overland to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what, if any, observations you made as you went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with the date, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was date that you visited Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was November 19 -- yes, November 19, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for reference to the diary, it's recorded on Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 3, page 60. Can you please describe your observations.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, en route to the city, immediately outside the city we could see the JNA gunners on their artillery pieces, the guns that were shelling the city. I should mention the city had fallen to the JNA forces, to the Serb forces the day previously. It fell on November 18. So we were there immediately after its capture. And then I toured the city. Perhaps I could read from my diary, with the Court's permission. It's only four lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think, for the record, it's on page 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, this portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote, just to describe the scene, I read from the diary here: "Do not see the downtown, but much of the town is seen nonetheless. Almost every building, every structure destroyed or shot at by shell-fire. A few destroyed tanks litter streets. Destruction everywhere."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to going to Vukovar, had General Kadijevic made representations to you as to what was the military objective of the siege on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you was the military objective?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: General Kadijevic said the purpose of the attack on Vukovar was to free a blockaded garrison of the JNA inside Vukovar. I must mention here, Counsel, excuse me, but I must mention that General Kadijevic was always exercised about the blockading of the JNA garrisons throughout Croatia, and it was, I would say, without question one of his principal concerns, and he raised it all the time with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of this, did you ask to be taken to see the garrison that had been blockaded?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe your observations of that garrison.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was a small garrison, a very small garrison. It was practically untouched, and I must say when one compared this small garrison that was almost untouched with the almost total destruction of the city around it, it was a shocking sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Secretary Vance tried to get into Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the principal purposes of the visit, because we had been alerted that a possible tragedy, indeed that a very bad situation was possible with the patients and people who were being held prisoner in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present with him when he attempted to gain access to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us what occurred when you tried to gain access to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He was physically prevented by the JNA major who was in command of the troops, and our escort, and a scene ensued, a very, very angry confrontation between Secretary Vance and this major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the major's name?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you were physically prevented from entering the hospital. Can you please describe more specifically how you were physically prevented.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Secretary Vance, who, incidentally, is a former US secretary of the army and has had a lot of experience with soldiers and he expected that his wishes would be observed, Sljivancanin physically blocked him; raised his rifle and would not let him pass. This occurred after there was some desultory conversation with Sljivancanin making a series of weak and obviously incorrect statements about mines being laid and the bridge being out, because the hospital lay across a bridge, a small bridge. And these were all total untruths. We could, for example, see the bridge was intact as Major Sljivancanin was telling us it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has seen on a number of occasions a rather famous piece of videotape. It's Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 10, and it depicts Secretary Vance arguing with Major Sljivancanin in Vukovar. Are you familiar with that piece of videotape?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I've seen several videos. I think there were probably more than one made. It was a continuous dispute between Secretary Vance and Major Sljivancanin, so I'm not quite sure which particular slice of the argument was shown, but I'm generally familiar with it. I was there at the time, so I know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While in Vukovar, did you make observations or record observations of Serb paramilitaries in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please relay to us your observations on that day.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: This -- I notice this up on the screen. It's immediately below the item we looked at on page 62. If I can read from it. It's brief. It's: "Visit to reception centre." And I wrote, and quote from the diary: "Many affecting scenes of weeping civilians, reunited families, et cetera. Secretary Vance talks to the displaced persons. Many foreign press on scene. The centre is full of JNA and many rough customers, armed irregulars, et al. An air of brooding and imminent menace conveyed by the Chetnik types." These were the irregulars and the paramilitaries who were intermingled with the JNA troops. They were standing, chatting with them, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. smoking cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these paramilitary troops, were they armed at the time they were intermingled with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, did you return to Belgrade after your visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We did not return directly. We went to Zagreb first, I notice from the diary, but we did go back to Belgrade two days later, yes. On November 21st we were back in Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you travelled in a JNA vehicle by land to Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to Serbia by land, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. As I mentioned - this is all in the diary so I don't need to take the time of Your Honours - we went to Zagreb and then to Sarajevo, and we flew from Sarajevo to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The time that you travelled from Belgrade to Vukovar, did you pass through a border control on the Serbian border?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. One had to do that in order to go from Yugoslavia to Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Chamber what, if any, border controls on the Serb side existed at that border control?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It was a heavily patrolled border. There were JNA troops there with checkpoints, also Serb police in their blue uniforms, which are different from the khaki of the JNA so they were immediately distinguishable. It was a border with border controls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it appear to you that the border controls, as they existed, did have the ability to effectively control people that were going back and forth across that border?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to Belgrade, did you have a meeting with General Veljko Kadijevic? I draw your attention to page 92 of the diary.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what date was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That was on November 21, 1991, at 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 3, page 92. Can you please summarise what occurred during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Secretary Vance had several important points he wanted to raise with General Kadijevic at this meeting. The first was the disproportionate damage, the enormous damage done to Vukovar, ostensibly to free the small garrison. The other point that Secretary Vance wanted to raise was our visit to the besieged Marsal Tito Kaserne in Zagreb where many JNA officers and their families were being effectively held hostage by the Croatians. And we had visited them and had a meeting with the officers, and Secretary Vance wanted to recount that to General Kadijevic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Kadijevic discuss with you or tell you about the fact that the Vukovar garrison had run out of food and water?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time later when you read an account of these events that contradicted what General Kadijevic had told you on this day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that account by?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That was by Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what Borisav Jovic said on this matter that contradicted what General Kadijevic told you regarding Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. In his memoir about the dissolution of Yugoslavia, a very bitter memoir, incidentally, Jovic, who had been a member of the Presidency and a very important Serb leader, he mentioned that the Vukovar garrison had been freed by the -- before the end of September, that it ceased being blockaded in September. He wrote that in his memoir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "memoir," are you referring to his book The Last Days of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you mentioned -- incidentally, are you mentioned and Secretary Vance, are your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remind me: Borisav Jovic, who is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He was the president of the Federal Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On what dates? About this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About this time, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that very same memoir, are some of the negotiations that you and Secretary Vance had, are they recorded from his perspective?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you read them?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I read the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they materially incorrect in any regard?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. I would not say that they were materially incorrect. They were rather nasty. He was bitter when he wrote this book, but he was a man of considerable authority as president of the country for a while and a major leader in Serbia, and he knew the situation. They are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that same day, the 21st of November, 1991, did you also have a meeting with Mr. Milosevic? I would draw your attention to page 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the Chamber, that would be Prosecution 397, tab 3, page 97.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please summarise that meeting for the Court.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Secretary Vance reported to the president on the horrific situation we had found in Vukovar. He was quite upset at the disproportionality of the damage done to the city and to the civilian population in it. He also raised the question of the unblocking of the garrisons with President Milosevic and a few other points as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about President Milosevic say regarding the siege of Vukovar or in response to what you described as your observations of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said the world would understand the destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he at some point change subjects to describe a person who was currently incarcerated in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, he discussed Goran Hadzic. I don't know that he was incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that he was. Please describe what he said regarding Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that Hadzic, whom we had already discussed before, was a nice young man, that he was the leader of Eastern Slavonia or the Eastern Krajina, as it was often referred to, and that he would welcome a peacekeeping force and that we wouldn't have any trouble with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador Okun, on the same page I noted that Mr. Milosevic referred to the Vukovar case as a "special case." Could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you locate the phrase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think what he meant, if I may, was that the destruction was unusually heavy. Vukovar was the most destroyed city during the entire fighting in Croatia, and I think that's what he was referring to as a "special case." And he perhaps also was thinking of the fact, which was undoubtedly true, that there were Serb civilians in the city as well. But I think basically he was talking about the disproportionate amount of the destruction compared with the ostensible reason for the destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, at this stage, November 1991, had yourself and Secretary Vance received any reports about Serb paramilitary activity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Secretary Vance raise that with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I note that I wrote down regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina: "I have heard disturbing reports of activities there by Serb irregulars." That's on page 98 of the diaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to read your entire entry regarding that discussion with Mr. Milosevic, and I would ask you to explain.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after Mr. Vance said that he had heard these disturbing reports, the diary continues: "Milosevic feigns surprise."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that your impression of Mr. Milosevic's reaction to being told this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe in a little greater detail what you meant when you wrote "feigns surprise."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was clear to me at the time, seemed clear to me at the time, that he knew what was going on - I couldn't imagine he didn't know what was going on - and he was pretending to be surprised at this report from Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to ask you one more question before the morning break. Prior to the end of this meeting, did Mr. Milosevic make one more representation to Secretary Vance and yourself regarding the JNA and Serbian irregulars?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. His concluding remarks at the meeting were that after the barracks were unblocked, which was General Kadijevic's principal concern, the release of the JNA troops, that the peacekeeping force could go into effect, and he said that we would have no problem with the JNA or Serbian irregulars with respect to keeping the peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- did you record that as a verbatim quote of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It's not within quotes in the diary, but it is written that way and those were the words. "Good. You will have no problem with JNA or Serbian irregulars."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's a convenient place to break for the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We will adjourn now for half an hour. Ambassador, I must formally tell you, don't speak to anybody about your evidence while you're giving it, please, until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Thank you. Could you be back in half an hour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, earlier this morning you told us that the culminating event or act of these initial missions to Yugoslavia was the signing of a cease-fire agreement that effectively ended the hostilities in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm now going to ask that you be shown a document, and it is tab 6 of Prosecution Exhibit 396. It's actually a three-page exhibit. I'm going to show you the last page of that exhibit. And do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recognise what that document that you have in your hands is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That is the Geneva Accord of November 23rd, 1991, which established the conditions for the cessation of hostilities in Croatia. There were four points, as you see; A, B, C, D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, before we go into the specifics of the document and so the record is complete, did you have an opportunity to see the first two pages of that exhibit earlier?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the first two pages of that exhibit are?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They're a transmittal note from the Secretary-General to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Providing the Security Council with this signed agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Correct, saying, "Here is the agreement of Mr. Vance for your information."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, given the importance of this document, I'm actually going to ask you to read it, and I would note for the Chamber and other parties in the court that it is on the screen so that they may see it. So, Ambassador, would you please read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "The undersigned --" May I say who signed it first?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It's signed by President Tudjman, President Milosevic, and General Kadijevic and Secretary Vance, and it says: "The following agree that (A) Croatia will, with immediate effect, lift its blockade of all JNA barracks and installations in Croatia; (B) the JNA will with immediate effect begin the withdrawal from Croatia of the personnel, weapons and military equipment in those barracks and installations and complete this process in accordance with the schedules already agreed upon by the parties; (C) they will immediately instruct all units under their command, control or political influence to observe an unconditional cease-fire with effect from tomorrow, 24 November, and they will make sure that any paramilitary or irregular units not formally under their command, control or political influence also observe the cease-fire from that date; (D) they will facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance to persons affected by the recent hostilities. Lord Carrington will seek to assure that the International Monitoring Mission does everything within its power and mandate to ensure that the cease-fire holds." Again signed by Presidents Tudjman, Milosevic, General Kadijevic, Cyrus Vance, Geneva, 23 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador this agreement, was it signed by anybody from the Federal Presidency, either the complete 8-person Presidency or the smaller Rump Presidency?
