utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. The only signatures are those that appear on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to go through each of the signatories and tell us, beginning with President Tudjman, what was his -- what people was his signature intended to commit and what was it intended to commit those people to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: President Tudjman, the president of Croatia, of the Republic of Croatia, committed the republic, by his signature, to the unblocking of the JNA garrisons and to the continued delivery of humanitarian assistance, paragraphs (A) and (D) of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Kadijevic, who was his signature intended to commit and what were they intended to be committed to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Essentially General Kadijevic was committing to paragraph (B) and to a lesser degree (C), principally (B) concerning the JNA withdrawal from the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic, who was his signature intended to commit and what was it intended that they be committed to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: President Milosevic's signature committed himself and the Yugoslav side to paragraphs (B), (C), and (D), namely the withdrawal of the JNA, the instructing of all political and military units, irregulars, and paramilitaries, in paragraph (C), to observe the cease-fire, and subparagraph (D), the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this discussed with Mr. Milosevic prior to his signing this agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, was that your interpretation or did Mr. Milosevic say something to that effect at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not an interpretation. It was Secretary Vance's and mine certain knowledge that he understood the terms of the Geneva Accord. Meetings took place in Geneva over a number of hours, and it is a brief and I think clear document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was referring to your comment that Mr. Milosevic committed himself to the agreement (B), for example. Did he say that at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, (D) or (E) did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (B), the JNA's withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had said it to us on repeated occasions, and it was understood that the signatures, particularly those of President Milosevic and President Tudjman, were controlling. They were the chiefs of state of their respective countries, and that was clear to all concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, were you actually present during the signing of this document?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I was present before and after. At this point, I think I was overseeing the reproduction of the document. I'm not sure whether I was present or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able today to identify to the Chamber which of these signatures belongs to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe it for us. Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it's the middle signature of the three across the top line, above the word "Cyrus Vance." Cyrus Vance appears below President Tudjman's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to a meeting with Mr. Milosevic on the 2nd of December, 1991. I'd ask you to take a look at your diaries. I believe it's in book 4. I would ask you to confirm whether or not you had a meeting with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might direct the Chamber's attention to Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 4, page 30.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did meet on December 2, for more than three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you characterise the purpose of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We returned to -- we returned to New York to report to the Secretary-General and the Security Council after the signature of the Geneva Accord on November 23rd and were back in Yugoslavia a week later, on December 1, and arrived and saw President Milosevic immediately upon our return, and the purpose was to discuss the situation on the ground in Croatia. Fighting was continuing, and we needed to continue serious talks on that situation and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic indicate to you that he had contacted someone the day after the signing -- the day after he signed this Geneva Accord?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the day after the signing of the Geneva Accord that he had been in touch with Hadzic and Babic, and he went on to say that they would respect the accord and that he had secured their consent. His words were, "I promised and I did," meaning, "I promised you, Mr. Vance, that I would secure their consent and I have done so."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the meeting with Mr. Milosevic that Secretary Vance raised the topic of the Dalmatian coast?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, he did. He asked the president what was happening because there was fighting along the Dalmatian coast, particularly around Dubrovnik, Zadar, and other Croatian cities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Milosevic say to Secretary Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that the Serbs had no links with Dalmatia and that, after the JNA barracks were unblocked in Croatia, that the army would leave Dubrovnik alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time did Secretary Vance raise with President Milosevic reports of Serb paramilitary activity in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did President Milosevic say?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He changed the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He changed the subject to what?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He told us that sometime earlier that Croatian troops had entered Pakrac - that's a town in Western Slavonia - that they had been wearing JNA uniforms and that they killed the people in Pakrac and generally committed mayhem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when Secretary Vance discussed with President Milosevic the possibility of continued violence from armed Serbs, meaning JNA paramilitary or local forces? Did there come a time when he discussed that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That happened and Secretary Vance was particularly concerned about the paramilitaries and the irregular Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read the relevant portions of your diary entry on this subject. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: On page 32, after that question was raised, President Milosevic said that with respect to the paramilitaries and the irregular forces, that the problem of control would not exist after a peacekeeping operation went into effect, that Goran Hadzic and Milan Babic would respect the commitments undertaken. Secretary Vance said that he trusted the president and that he looked to him to deliver them. That is to say he looked to President Milosevic to make sure that Babic and Hadzic would comply with the terms of the peacekeeping operation, and President Milosevic replied, "I will use my influence. I am not their master, but I am sure they will fulfil what they promise." And that -- and Secretary Vance, after that, re-read the section from the Geneva Accord that concerned the paramilitaries, because he knew that Mr. Milosevic was in control of and responsible for the paramilitaries. And you will note on page 93, next to the phrase, "CRV reads from Geneva accord."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 33, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me, I'm sorry. Forgive me. Page 33. Vance, in parentheses, "reads from Geneva Accord regarding paramilitaries," et cetera, et cetera. And that was to get on the record and to reiterate his knowledge to President Milosevic as to who controlled the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Milosevic say when or after Secretary Vance read that portion of the Geneva Accord?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: President Milosevic said that they are -- he claimed that they were observing the cease-fire and that one small group, a harmless group, had made a statement opposing the cease-fire. He also went on to say that nobody was attacking Osijek, and he stated that Serbs had been slaughtered in Vukovar and that mass graves or, as he called them, collective graves had just been found. That's on page 33.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic ever indicate specifically where these collective graves containing these Serb victims was specifically located?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, he did not to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I want to draw your attention to -- I'm sorry. Did Mr. Milosevic go on to make some statement regarding Hadzic's control over paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that Hadzic had them under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he give a percentage of the paramilitaries that were under the control of Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that with respect to the paramilitaries and territorials, that 95 per cent of them were local territorials, that they were well organised, but that Hadzic had them under his control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of this meeting, did the issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina arise?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who initiated the change of subject to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At this meeting, the subject of Bosnia and Herzegovina was begun by President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe what it was he said about Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it was unfair to listen only to President Izetbegovic and that it was important, in order to be successful with respect to the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and here, parenthetically, one has to recall that at this time there was, as yet, no fighting in Bosnia. He said that to be successful, one had to talk to all sides. And Mr. Vance asked him for help in meeting the other side, the Bosnian Serbs, obviously. And that was the initial exchange on Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Milosevic name a particular person who he suggested he needed to speak to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that it was important to talk to the Serb leaders, and this was Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first time you had heard the name Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ask --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I must amend that. It was not the first time I had heard the name. I had never written it down myself. I hadn't written it, but I had heard the name, yes. In October of 1991, two months earlier, I was in Sarajevo during a meeting of the parliament and when the Bosnian Serbs left the parliament, and Karadzic's name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to Secretary Vance, President Milosevic, and yourself, was there anybody else present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. President Milosevic had with him a Mr. Jovanovic, the Foreign Minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did somebody actually write the name Karadzic into your diaries here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I see it on page 40. "Mr. Karadzic" is written in Latin script. Not by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was either Jovanovic or President Milosevic. Probably Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Milosevic agree to set up a meeting between Secretary Vance, yourself, and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he in fact set up such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take to arrange this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was -- took practically no time at all. We finished our meeting with President Milosevic and Jovanovic at lunch, a pleasant lunch, at 3.30 p.m., and at 5.00, we met with Karadzic. So it was almost immediate. A couple of hours at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We met him in a house in a suburb of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall how you got to that house?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We were taken there, as I recollect, in a government car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about this portion or this meeting with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I refer the Chamber to Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 4, page 44.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please summarise what occurred during this meeting with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, this was our first meeting with Radovan Karadzic, and we wanted to hear him, probe his views on the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, size him up because it was our first face-to-face meeting, and in general, we also wanted to explain to him the possible peacekeeping operation that was planned for Croatia. Again, I repeat, there was no fighting at this time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the topic of Slovenia arise during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in the meeting did the topic of Slovenia arise?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Right at the beginning. It was practically the first thing that Karadzic raised with us was the issue of recognition of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say with respect to the recognition of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said he thought it was a good idea. He didn't care about Slovenia leaving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he allude to any specific action he was going to take in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was going to put forward the idea in the Serb parliament - by that he meant the Bosnian Serb parliament - to recognise Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I want to leave this meeting now and ask you, on the 3rd of December, 1991, did you and Secretary Vance make a visit to Osijek?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe where you went on that journey.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We again went via the JNA military facilities, on land, through Novi Sad. We crossed the Danube River into Croatia, and we reached Dalj, which was JNA headquarters in Croatia for that region. It was where the corps commander was who was in charge of the JNA troops that surrounded Osijek and were attacking the city. The command was in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to embarking on this trip, had you been given reports from the JNA and other Serb authorities regarding the condition or activities in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We had been told that the Croatians had destroyed Dalj and that it was in terrible shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your observations of the condition of the city?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't true at all. It had hardly been touched. It was in quite normal condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave Dalj and go on to Osijek?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We went through the frontlines by agreement of the two armies. We had to cross across the frontline, and we reached the point where the JNA handed us over to the Croatians, and we -- an incident occurred at the -- during the crossover, but we went between the two contending armies on land, and by foot, I may say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I've omitted to ask you a question: Before leaving Dalj, did you have a conversation with the JNA commander there regarding who was shelling Osijek?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He gave us a, I would say a thorough briefing - it lasted almost an hour - on the military situation, and he said that there was no JNA artillery shelling and that there had not been any since the cease-fire agreement of November 23. He did say, since the city was obviously being shelled, that territorials, Serb territorials from the Baranja, that is from the Serb side of the Danube, were shelling -- were shelling Osijek. Osijek lies on the western bank of the Danube River, which forms the border between Serbia and Croatia at that point. It's a large city, the capital of Eastern Slavonia. So it was easily targetable from the Serb side. It was just across the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the record is clear, when you're using the term "Serb side," did you take it that the JNA commander was referring to shelling coming from the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He made that clear. He used the term "the Baranja," and there was no doubt in his mind or ours what he was telling us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I interrupted you when you were referring to an incident that occurred on your way to Osijek. Could I ask you to please tell us what incident you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were being taken, as I said, between the sides. We were actually driving, being driven in a -- in a -- at that point in an ECMM vehicle, that is the European Community monitors. We had a Danish driver and an Italian observer, and we were sitting in the back seat of what was basically a minivan and going very slowly down the road. And the fellow in the second seat yelled out, "Stop," and the driver Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stopped the van, and stretched across the road was a very thin wire attached to a mine. Somebody had mined the road. We never found out who. We got out of the van, inspected. I went up to the wire, which was a sort of thin wire, and one of the EC monitors, I don't remember whether it was the Dane or the Italian, destroyed it, not by clipping it, because he thought that would set the mine off because he had inspected the side of the road and there was indeed a mine there, on both sides, but he burned the wire with his cigarette lighter in order not to create any vibration, and then he removed the wire and we walked the rest of the way, which was less than a mile at this point, into Osijek, to be safe. And it was, of course, an interesting moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, on this day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic had a point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wish to assist Mr. Okun in relation to the geography mentioned. Actually, Baranja is not in Serbia. The gentleman from the other side asked him whether this was on the Serbian side. Baranja is not in Serbia. If you remember, he showed us that Maslenica was on the island of Solta. It would be a good idea if you'd have a look at the map, if you'd see where Osijek is, on which river, who could have shelled it, and what the JNA officer could have said. I think that Mr. Groome is actually misleading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not. He's not. He's not, and we have a map so we can look at it. Yes, Mr. Groome, go on with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll have the map brought out so the ambassador can indicate precisely where he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, on this day did you have occasion to see a person who you came to know as, or came to learn his identity was Arkan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe the circumstances under which you saw him.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. As we were leaving the briefing by the JNA corps commander in Dalj, we left his headquarters, which were actually in a church, and in the churchyard, milling around, were journalists and troops, and one of the Western journalists came up to me and said that Arkan was standing a dozen or so feet away, about as near as you and I are standing, and would Mr. Vance and I like to meet him. And we respectfully declined that invitation to meet Arkan, but we saw him and his troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe whether or not they were armed.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. They were carrying sidearms and long weapons, and they were intermingled with the JNA troops. They were standing about, talking with each other, smoking. You know, just generally fraternising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they dressed differently than the JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They were in uniforms, as I recall, most of them, but they were not turned out smartly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 336, page 23. It's simply a map of the area. I'm going to ask that be placed on the overhead. I'm then going to ask you to take a pointer and indicate to the Chamber -- first of all, I'd ask you to indicate Dalj, if it is on that map. If you look to your left, Ambassador, the original is on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Dalj, as you see, is on the river to the south-east of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you point to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Osijek is a few miles down the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the JNA commander in Dalj indicated to you that the shelling of Osijek was coming from the Serb side, can you indicate where on this map you understood him to be referring to.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, you see the line of the Danube where I'm moving the pointer; that's the border. You see the town of Apotin on the Serb side. You see directly to the east of Osijek, between Dalj and Osijek, a town called Sarvas. That's where we crossed the frontline. That's noted in my diary that we crossed the frontline. I believe it's in the diary. And this is -- Osijek itself is physically on the Drava. So this is a very small area, and that is the area that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you indicate where it was the JNA commander indicated that shelling -- the shelling of Osijek was coming from.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said it was coming from the territorials. Now, they could have been based at Darda or Belija [phoen], north of the city. I was never there, I didn't see it. They also could have been just across the other side of the Danube. The distance is -- it's about 10 or 11 kilometres from Osijek to the border. That's six miles. But six miles is within artillery range, so they could have been north of the city, or they could have been south or east. The distances are all very small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In any case, we saw the JNA artillery. Speaking of artillery, we saw and I noted in my diary, if I may, at the bottom of 52 -- not to belabour the point on artillery but if I could just draw your attention to the very bottom of page 52 where I noted in the diary, and I quote: "The road --" this is where we go through the frontlines just west of Sarvas. "Road goes through flat, cornbelt terrain, stalks withering in fields. A few farmhouses here and there. A fair amount of JNA artillery batteries sitting in the cornfields. At one point a trench meanders away from the road, a la World War I." So there was artillery all around the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your visit to Osijek, did you go visit the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We made a thorough tour. I did. I think Secretary Vance at one point stayed behind, but we both went to the hospital and I made a complete tour of the city, at my request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, in a sentence or two, to describe the general condition of the hospital in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The hospital was in very bad shape. It was next to the river. It had been shelled heavily. It was a modern hospital, about five or six stories high, and every story above ground had been completely shattered. It was not used at all. I mean, there was glass and rubble everywhere. The hospital, however, had underground facilities. Two or three stories underground were completely equipped because it had been built to withstand an attack in case, you know, Yugoslavia were ever invaded from the northeast by the Soviet army, through Hungary. And so the hospital had underground facilities, and they were functioning. Indeed, we visited the maternity ward where children, babies had been born recently, but the hospital above the ground was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to now draw your attention to the 31st of December, 1991. Did you have a meeting with President Milosevic and Foreign Minister Jovanovic on that day? And I would refer you to your book number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the Chamber, this would be Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 5, page 61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 31st. Yes. We met in the morning for two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We would have met in President Milosevic's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please summarise that meeting for us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the meeting began with the president himself summarising the situation with respect to the possible creation of the peacekeeping operation, and he said that all representatives, that is all Serbian representatives, including Babic, would agree in writing to the peacekeeping plan, which by this point we had formalised and written down for the parties, that is for the Croats and for the Serbs. And he went on to say that the announcement by the state committee, which was headed by Borisav Jovic, the state committee for peacekeeping, would be made today accepting the -- Secretary Vance's suggestion for a UN peacekeeping operation. When we asked him what would happen if another Babic appeared, that is to say if suddenly some paramilitary suddenly emerged to oppose the UN, President Milosevic said it would not happen. He assured Mr. Vance that no such person would appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to indicate, for the record again, it's on page 59 instead of 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm very sorry. I think I have to put on my glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, would it be fair to say that after the signing of the Geneva Accord, the cessation of hostilities, the primary efforts of Secretary Vance and yourself were to come up with a detailed plan of the peacekeeping force and then to work towards its implementation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That was -- yes. That was one of two major efforts. The other major effort which was, I have to say, more difficult, was to gain Croatian acceptance to the final and definitive unblocking of the JNA barracks throughout Croatia. So those were the two principal efforts post November 23, 1991. On the one side, secure cooperation and agreement to the peacekeeping plan; on the other side, secure Croatian agreement to unblocking the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that prior to the actual implementation of the UN peacekeepers, Secretary Vance and yourself were monitoring whether the cease-fire signed on the 23rd of November, whether that was holding, whether the parties were still willing to observe the agreement that President Tudjman, President Milosevic, and General Kadijevic signed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the primary person who you sought to confirm that -- the parties representing the Serb side, who was the person that you sought or spoke to to confirm whether they were still willing to observe their obligations under the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to this meeting of the 31st of December, did there come a time during this meeting when President Milosevic once again raised the subject of minority rights as described in the original Carrington Draft Convention, the one of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was in connection with a discussion of the problems of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please summarise the discussion between President Milosevic and Secretary Vance on that subject.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was a lengthy discussion, as I noted in my diary, and the essence of the discussion, which was not the first time it had been discussed, was the treatment of the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. The position taken by Secretary Vance, by Lord Carrington, and others was that if in the second chapter of Carrington's AGS, that is the document of October 18, the settlement for the former Yugoslavia, that if in that document the Serb people were given special status in Croatia, that in fairness, Serbia should grant the same status to the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. President Milosevic differed and pointed out that the Serbian people were a constituent people, not a minority, and that the Yugoslav constitution and historical practice in the former Yugoslav space gave special rights to the constituent peoples who could not be considered minorities. I should add he was correct in that statement, because the constituent peoples did have particular rights under the 1974 constitution. That, however, did not mean that other peoples were not to be treated in a humane fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I draw your attention now to the 2nd of January, 1992. What occurred on that day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: On that day, the accord implementing the cease-fire, the implementing accord, was signed in Sarajevo, and that brought about a cessation of hostilities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, a number of witnesses have appeared before the Tribunal and referred to the Vance Plan. Would I be correct in saying that it's a bit of a misnomer that there is a single document that one can look at and say, "This is the Vance Plan"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that is a misnomer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber the documents that together comprise what people commonly refer to as the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It is a complicated subject, but let me be brief. People mean by the Vance Plan the peacekeeping operation in Croatia. The four documents that established what they called the Vance Plan but what Secretary Vance himself never did, nor did I, were four. The cessation -- the cease-fire agreement -- the cease-fire agreement of November 23, 1991, and its implementing accord of January 2, 1992. Those were the two documents that determined the situation on the ground, the cessation of hostilities. The other two documents were the concept paper for the peacekeeping operation, the technical details of the operation, where the UNPAs would be, that sort of thing, how they would be policed. That was the concept paper of December 3. And the final document was the Security Council Resolution that established the peacekeeping operation, Resolution 743 of February 21. So you have November 23, January 1, the cessation of hostilities agreement. December 3, peacekeeping operation details. February 21, 1992, Security Council Resolution establishing it. Those four documents taken together were the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you've already identified the cessation of hostilities or the Geneva accord for us. I'm now going to ask that you be shown three other documents. Perhaps to save time, if the usher is willing to carry all three to the witness box, I'd ask that you first be shown tab 7 of Prosecution Exhibit 396. I'd ask you to take a look at it and identify it if you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only five tabs. I did not have the sixth one, and now the seventh one is being referred to, so I really don't know. It was my understanding that this is 396 and then tabs 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar is coming to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I will provide my copies, Your Honour, in the interim. Your Honour, we're providing Mr. Milosevic with another set of the documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is 396.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 396. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have a look at the documents you were just given, Mr. Milosevic. 396, tab 7. What we're looking at is the concept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I only got the first part, with five tabs, and these start with tab 6 and then go on to 7, 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, this is the concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is the concept plan for the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you to take a look at tab 8. Can you identify that document for us?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, tab 8, number 147 on the document, under numbers 147, dated Sarajevo, 2 January 1992 is the text of the implementing accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, could you please take a look at tab 9 of Prosecution Exhibit 396.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, tab 9 is Resolution 743 of the Security Council, dated 21 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, to save some time, I'd like to jump ahead to a meeting you had on the 15th of April, 1992. I believe it is in book 7 of your diaries, and I would draw the Court's attention to 397, tab 7, page 39. It's the 15th of April, on page 39. Did you have a meeting with Mr. Milosevic on that day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see we did. Mr. Vance and myself met with President Milosevic and Jovanovic for about -- almost three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please summarise what transpired during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, by this time the conflict had spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Fighting had begun there in March, after the referendum was held, and we were very concerned about that. The situation was worsening on the ground. Lord Carrington's Conference on Yugoslavia was continuing to struggle, as it turned out unsuccessfully, to reach an agreement, and Secretary Vance was very concerned with the reports that we had received about the activity of Serbian paramilitaries and irregulars in Bosnia on the eastern -- along the eastern border of the Drina, separating Bosnia from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that discussed in detail with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Secretary Vance raised the question and asked, and one sees this on page 41, "What about Arkan on the Drina? General Adzic says he's there." Meaning what about Arkan on the Bosnian side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did President Milosevic say?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said that was not the case. He said no, that perhaps somebody else was there but that it was completely prohibited to go out of Serbia and that Arkan was advertising himself on TV that he had been privately, privately, in Bijeljina, in the north-eastern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, in this statement, did you take this as an admission by President Milosevic that he was aware of Arkan's presence in the Bosnian municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean when he said that Arkan was there privately?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, I think we understood the common sense of that, namely that he had gone there on his own hook, under his own authority, and that nobody except Arkan was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please continue from that portion in the diary with what occurred next.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it's clear from the diary that Secretary Vance did not believe that, because his next words were: "No. That won't wash." That was what Vance said to the president. And then President Milosevic responded: "Only at the beginning -" meaning that Arkan was there only at the beginning of the fighting - "the rest of the time he was in Belgrade." And Vance, it's clear from the diary, and this is recording the interchange as it occurred, did not enjoy hearing that answer because he says: "Let me be frank: People I trust have seen Arkan and other Serbian types with heavy equipment," meaning along the Drina in Bosnia. "Why is this happening?" That's what the diary records. And President Milosevic replied to that: "Only some individuals not in control of the Serbian authorities. We forbid paramilitaries," and President Milosevic went on to say: "Arkan was only in Bijeljina at the beginning." Vance shows his disbelief of that assertion by saying: "To be perfectly frank, you and Serbia are being hurt. If this continues, it will have a very negative effect on Serbian recognition and derecognition," that is to say on the recognition by the United Nations and the world of Serbia, and derecognising -- unrecognising them, that is, declaring them an outlaw state. And President Milosevic agrees. He says: "I agree we are being hurt." And then he pleads for understanding, by saying: "We cannot check on every Serb." And Secretary Vance continues this difficult discussion by saying: "You have a real problem. You have to clean it up." And you'll notice, Your Honours, that I wrote in capital letters in the diary, "Clean it up." And then Secretary Vance, who was a gentleman, said to the president, "I speak as a friend."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you to continue on the next page of your diary and relay the remainder of that conversation between Secretary Vance and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the secretary says to the president that: "You have got to push through..." that is to say, implement the April 12th Cutilheiro agreement. This is on page 43. "... and see that it is implemented in letter and spirit." As I mentioned earlier, Ambassador Cutilheiro was working on a Bosnian peace plan under the direction of Lord Carrington. So that's what he means by the Cutilheiro agreement. There was an actual peace plan. President Milosevic reiterated that: "No one is in Bosnia and Herzegovina from Serbia." And Secretary Vance, reading from his prepared talking points that we had worked on before the meeting, tells

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Serbia cannot hope to win a military victory in Bosnia either directly or surreptitiously." That is to say, they cannot win it directly via the JNA or surreptitiously via the paramilitaries and the irregulars. You see, Secretary Vance was thoroughly aware of the use of the paramilitaries and the irregulars in tandem but covertly under control. And President Milosevic agreed and says: "That's right." And asks rhetorically of us: "Do you think I want a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And Secretary Vance responds: "It looks that way." And President Milosevic responds that the Croatian army started the fighting in Bosnia. You see "CA" for Croatian army, started by invading over the bridge into Bosanski Brod, written "Bos Brod," Bosanski Brod. And he reiterated his point that nobody could push the Serbs into, as he called it, "that mess." Vance responded that: "Everyone knows that Arkan was there." And President Milosevic admitted this and said: "Yes. But others are in Bosnia as well."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to now draw your attention to the next day, the 16th of April, 1992. Did you have a meeting with Radovan Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic during which the subject of Sarajevo arose?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- and I'm referring to Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 7, page 69. Can I ask you to briefly summarise in a sentence or two what was said in terms of Sarajevo in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Koljevic, Nikola Koljevic, said that just that day, April 16, 1992, he and Karadzic had agreed that we should divide Sarajevo, meaning we, the Bosnian Serbs, should divide Sarajevo into a Serb area and a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Koljevic was saying that on that very day, the 16th of April, the decision was taken between him and Karadzic to divide Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to the 6th of May, 1992. Did you have a meeting with Mr. Milosevic and Bulatovic? And this would be Prosecution Exhibit 397, tab 7, page 140.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We met with the president and President Bulatovic from Montenegro. They were accompanied by their foreign ministers, Jovanovic and Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that meeting, did Lord Carrington confront President Milosevic with reports about Serb activity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And not only Bosnia but also the Krajina, that is in Croatia, in Kosovo and the Vojvodina province of Serbia. That's on page 140 of my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did you record Mr. Milosevic's response to Lord Carrington's query?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. President Milosevic responded by saying that all Serbs and the JNA would be out of Bosnia-Herzegovina within two weeks and that Bosnia was not within the competence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that he, President Milosevic, supported the talks on Bosnia and Herzegovina. That would be the talks being conducted by Cutilheiro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Milosevic used the term "all Serbs and the JNA," who did you understand him to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Clearly he was talking about the paramilitaries and the irregulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Otherwise, he would have just said "the JNA." I mean, he wasn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. talking about Serb civilians or tourists. There was no question that, you know, the hundreds of thousands of Serbs were not going to leave Bosnia. So he was talking about the irregulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cutilheiro go on to describe to Mr. Milosevic specific reports of paramilitary activity in the Bosnian municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Cutilheiro said that, in Foca, Serb irregulars had committed terrible acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Milosevic's response?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said it wasn't up to us. You know, he said, "We just want to finish the talks." I regarded that as a routine disclaimer and so note it in the diary, on page 141. "We --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador -- please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We want to finish talks on Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not up to us. (Routine disclaimer)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, on page 140, I noted a phrase said by

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "We are one delegation. It's a fact." Could you make an observation on that comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was referring to the fact that he was present with the president of Montenegro, which was a republic, but he was -- wanted to make the point that they should be seen as one delegation, one country, not two. That, incidentally, was also our understanding, that Serbia and Montenegro were one delegation. The reason for that, Your Honour, is that only about ten days earlier, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, Tito's Yugoslavia, had officially gone out of existence, and the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the FRY, had come into existence. The FRY consisted of Serbia and Montenegro, and President Milosevic was recording that fact for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, would I be correct in saying that around this period of time, your work on the Vance missions was winding down and your work on the ICFY missions was beginning to start up?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, because the war in Bosnia had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to a few diary entries in your ICFY journals or diaries, and the first one I'd like to draw your attention to would be a meeting on the 9th of October, 1992, and this would be Prosecution Exhibit 398, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the -- Ambassador Okun did not number the pages in the ICFY journals as he did in the Vance mission, so the reference will be the date and the time. I would direct your attention to the 9th of October, 1992, at 5.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, Ambassador, is did you have a meeting with Radovan Karadzic on that day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, what day are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October -- I'm sorry, Ambassador, I'm getting reversed with that, the American system and the European system. September 10, 1992. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: September 10, 1992. Yes, we did meet with Karadzic and a Bosnian Serb colonel, Zarkovic, and I note he had with him a note-taker, Karadzic, yes. October -- excuse me. September 10, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the topic of Sarajevo discussed in detail during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Radovan Karadzic explain to yourself and Secretary Vance his rationale for what was going on in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, when you say "what was going on," you mean the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe that interchange for us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, he said quite a lot about Sarajevo. He said, among other things, that it was the biggest concentration camp in all of Bosnia, that 60.000, 80.000 Serbs were being held hostage there. He typically ranted and raved, if I may say, on that subject with great frequency. And he also gave us his account of what we considered - what I considered, at any rate - his personal reasons for the shelling of the city. He stated it directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you record that in the diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what he said now.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said, yes, that -- again -- he said that Sarajevo was the biggest camp, meaning concentration camp, and I believe he said -- yes, here it is. He actually said that "They" - meaning the Bosnian government - "started the war by expelling me from my apartment in Sarajevo," and that they tortured 80.000 Serbs. I quote from the diary: "They started the war by expelling me from my apartment in Sarajevo. Tortured 80.000 Serbs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Lord Owen respond to him at that point?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Lord Owen shut him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he then give his rationale for the situation or his understanding of the military situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said very seriously, he said: "Look, we --" meaning the Bosnian Serbs -- "we are 35 per cent," meaning 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia. "They are 65 per cent. We have the weapons. They have the men. If we give up weapons and they don't give up men, we are doomed." Those were his words. And it indicated to us that he had no intention of giving up the weapons nor any intention of stopping the shelling of the city, and unfortunately, that proved to be the case until, by force, they were stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, would I be correct in saying that a fair amount of your time working on the ICFY meetings and discussions, that Sarajevo formed the basis of many of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself keep track of reports of the shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, because, while we were in Geneva, I received on a daily basis the shell count from the UN observers who were posted in and around Sarajevo. That is to say, the incoming shells from the Serb artillery onto the city and the outgoing fire from the Muslim side in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you record these daily reports that you received of these shelling counts?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I kept a graph on the wall of my office in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise the picture that developed over the time that you kept these records regarding the ratio of outgoing shells from Sarajevo as opposed to incoming shells.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The average daily incoming shell-fire, that is from the Serb artillery being rained into the city, was between 4 and 5.000 shells per day. The response fire from the Bosnian government was 300 or 400, of much smaller calibre, it has to be noted. So it was a ratio of about 10 to 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your discussions with the various parties on the subject of Sarajevo, did you form an impression of the objectives of the Serb side regarding the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly summarise that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I thought the Bosnian Serbs had three major objectives with regard to the shelling of Sarajevo: First, to tie down the Bosnian government army in the defence of their capital; second, to carry out the Bosnian Serb plan to physically divide the city by, so to speak, by a wall of fire that would divide the population via the shell-fire; and third, to frighten the Bosnian government, which of course was resident in the city, to frighten them and so to discourage them that they would sign a peace term on Bosnian Serb terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, a few minutes ago you made reference to Radovan Karadzic beginning to discuss 80.000 tortured Serbs. Was one of the ostensible goals articulated by the Bosnian Serb leadership regarding Sarajevo, was one of the ostensible goals to protect Serbs living in Sarajevo, in the besieged city?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was a constant theme of Karadzic, Koljevic, and when we saw him, Krajisnik as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and Secretary Vance attempt to verify, by talking to humanitarian organisations, the state or the condition of Serbs living or having remained within the city?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, and we also were in Sarajevo ourselves. We visited the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you learnt about the condition of Serbs living in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, they were no worse off than anybody else. Everybody in Sarajevo was living under constant shell-fire, gunfire. It was a terribly difficult situation. The world knew that; it was heavily reported in the press and on television. But there was no mass mistreatment of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to now draw your attention to a meeting on September 17, 1992, with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would draw the Chamber's attention to Prosecution Exhibit 398, and I will give the Chamber the evidence record number. That probably is the best way to reference it now. I would draw your attention to R0163952.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I want to draw your attention to a portion of that meeting. Did Secretary Vance discuss with Radovan Karadzic Serb -- Bosnian Serb irregulars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Ambassador, could you please tell us, where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, this meeting was in Geneva on September 17th. It began at 9 -- 10.00 p.m. and ended at 10.05 p.m. It was in the evening, in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what if anything was said on the subject of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Secretary Vance raised the question and asked: "What about your irregular troops? Who controls them?" And Karadzic replied that perhaps 5 per cent were not under control but that he controlled the rest, meaning he controlled 95 per cent of the Bosnian Serb irregulars. And he went on to say, and I quoted him in the diary, and I read: "We can do anything. Army has unified command. I have full power." That's what Radovan Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he go on later in the meeting to suggest to you and Secretary Vance what was necessary to end the conflict in all of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the war would not end, that it could not be stopped until the other sides, by which he meant the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, were pressured into stopping fighting. He said that what were needed were sanctions against the Bosnian Croats and that it was necessary to derecognise the Muslims, because by this time, as we all know, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had formally received international recognition. So this was Dr. Karadzic in effect Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. demanding that the international community unrecognise the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Clearly an impossibility, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make reference to the parties that you needed to gather around the table that were necessary to resolve the conflict, end the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that Mr. Vance and Lord Owen could end the war, that if they brought around one table and on one side of the table President Milosevic and Hadzic and he were sitting together, that is to say President Milosevic, Hadzic of Croatia, and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, if they were on one side of the table, and on the other side of the table sat President Tudjman of Croatia and Mate Boban, the leader of the Bosnian Croats, that they together could solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a notable omission to the people that he suggested be gathered around the table?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: There were no Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, in order to save time, I'm going to skip over a number of other meetings, but I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to them, and I believe that they will be self-explanatory if read by the Chamber. They would be a meeting on the 2nd of October, 1992, a meeting with Radovan Karadzic; a meeting on the 11th of October, 1992, also with Mr. Karadzic; and again a meeting on the 6th of January, 1993, with Mr. Milosevic. And I will provide the evidence record number as soon as possible with respect to those specific entries. I want to now draw your attention to a meeting you had with Momcilo Krajisnik on the 11th of January, 1993. I'd ask you to open your diary to that meeting. This would be Prosecution Exhibit 398, and the diary entry 11 of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, did he articulate three major features that any plan would have to contain in order to be acceptable to the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And may I add that Karadzic and General Mladic were also present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what were the three conditions that he articulated?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that first, Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be a composite state, that is a state with separate entities, made up of separate units, separate entities, that that was necessary. It could not be a unitary state. Second, he stated that it was important for the Bosnian Serbs, that is to say the Bosnian Serb entity, to have relations with other states, and of course he and we understood that meant principally Serbia. And his third point was that the Bosnian Serb entity, Bosnian Serb state within a state, had to have territorial continuity, that is it could not be chopped up into smaller bits. It had to be one coherent territorial state. Those were his three conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this conversation with Mr. Krajisnik, did, over the course of your negotiations with Bosnian Serb leaders, these and other conditions or aims emerge as primary and essential aims from their point of view to stop the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serbs had six war aims, several in addition to these, that they were consistent with these, but they had basically six war aims which were known, stated privately to us, but were known publicly to those who followed events closely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please go through each of those six and explain each one to us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The six Bosnian Serb war aims were as follows: First, the creation of Republika Srpska; that is to say, a separate Bosnian Serb entity which they called Republika Srpska, the Serbian Republic. Second, that Republika Srpska have a continuous geographical integrity, as we just mentioned, that it be a coherently geographic state. Third, that it be pure Serb. Almost exclusively Serb ethnic, and that, of course, was what explained the ethnic cleansing. The fourth point was that the Bosnian Serb state, Republika Srpska, had to have a special relationship with Serbia, as Mr. Krajisnik mentioned explicitly at that meeting. And by a special relationship it was understood to be that they could trade and even recognise each other. This was sometimes referred to by Western diplomats as a parallel relationship, which was not an incorrect term, and it -- what it implied was that their relationship, this special or parallel relationship would be independent of the relationship that the central government in Sarajevo could have with countries around the world, independent. The fifth point was that the Bosnian Serbs wanted a veto power over any important decisions made by a residual central government in Sarajevo, because they knew there would be a central government, some nominal central government in Sarajevo. And the sixth and last point was to divide Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, these aims that you've just described for us, would it be fair to say that they emerged during the context of trying to develop the Vance-Owen Peace Plan for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. They emerged during the course of the conference. They were known previously during the Cutilheiro time, during Lord Carrington's time, but they became explicitly clear to Lord Owen and Secretary Vance as they sought to develop a peaceful settlement for the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- your work in ICFY culminate with the presentation to the parties of a Vance-Owen Peace Plan for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It was presented to the parties formally at a conference in Geneva over a series of days in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that peace plan grant the Bosnian Serbs any of the aims that you've articulated for us here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Actually, no. It rejected all six Bosnian Serb demands explicitly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please briefly describe for the Chamber the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and what ultimately happened to the plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The plan called for a single Bosnian state internationally recognised within its borders, organised on a decentralised basis. It had ten provinces in the country. There was no Republika Srpska. It called for the total demilitarisation of the country. It called for the highest standards of human rights within the country and set up a court system overseen by non-Bosnian judges to make the final decision on human rights, and then a whole series of military measures as well. The provinces were consciously not drawn on an ethnic basis. Of the ten provinces, six had no ethnic majority whatsoever. Of course, the negotiators were dealing with a real country. They weren't drawing lines on the moon, and so some provinces had more Serbs and some had more Muslims and some had more Croats, but the point was to maintain as much as possible of an ethnic balance. Indeed, one of the principal Bosnian Serb objections, one of the points that they were furious about, was that most of the Bosnian Serbs under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan would have resided outside of provinces in which Bosnian Serbs were a majority. This, I must say, was a very big sticking point for them. With respect to the acceptance of the plan, the Bosnian Croats accepted the plan immediately on its presentation. The Bosnian Muslim side accepted it a bit later, after some changes were made in the map and in the arrangements for an interim administration between the adoption of the plan and the time that it entered into effect. They wanted to make sure they stayed in control of the central government, which Vance and Owen agreed to. The Bosnian Serbs never accepted the plan, except that, under very heavy pressure, Karadzic did sign the plan in May 1993 at a meeting in Athens. He signed it subject to, as he put it, approval by the Bosnian Serb parliament. But when he returned to Bosnia a few weeks later, the Bosnian Serb parliament, as expected, rejected the plan. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So in sum, it was accepted by the Bosnian Croats, accepted by the Bosnian Muslims, and rejected by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was President Milosevic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to have to bring this to a close. We have to be out sharply at quarter to. Could you give us, Mr. Groome, an exhibit number, when we next return, for the Vance-Owen Plan. I think we have it exhibited in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour it's tab 6, 7, 8, and 9 of Prosecution Exhibit 396. I'm sorry. I'm thinking of the Vance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's been exhibited, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's tab 10, Your Honour, in 396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have the evidence record numbers of the meetings I was referring the Chamber to. If the Chamber wishes, I can just give it to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would. Thank you very much. Now, the position tomorrow, we're expecting General Mangan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And then on Friday I have approximately a half hour of questions for the ambassador to conclude my examination of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the other witness going to take all day tomorrow or can we ask this witness to come back later in the morning and try to finish more of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's unclear but I think the best thing is to have the witness available so he may be telephoned before the last of the two breaks and come in then if it seems appropriate. It would be desirable to take the other half hour of examination-in-chief tomorrow if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well clearly that would be helpful in order to try to finish the witness on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, it has to be noted I think Friday is a slightly longer session than today but it's only limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ambassador, you heard that exchange. If you would be available tomorrow morning on the end of a telephone, at least. We'll see how we get on with the other witness, and if we can, we'll continue with your evidence tomorrow. We will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
